Silent H, so there’s liaison: “neuf heures” = “nuh-VUR”, “deux heures” = “duh-ZUR”, “trois heures” = “trwa-ZUR”, “six heures” = “see-ZUR”, “dix heures” = “dee-ZUR”.
VINGT alone = “vẽ”. “Vingt et un” = “vẽ-tay-ẽ”, “vingt-deux” = “vẽt-duh” (you hear the t from 21 to 29). But “quatre-vingts” = “katr-vẽ”, no t.
AI and AIS are read as an open “e”, as in “bed”: je vais = “zhuh VEH”, français = “frahn-SEH”, mais = “meh”.
All days except “dimanche” end in -di, Latin for “day”: lun-DI (Moon day, like Monday), mar-DI (Mars’ day), mercre-DI (Mercury’s day).
QU is read “k”: quatre = “katr”, quart = “kar”, quelle = “kel”. The u is silent.
ALLER ends in -er, but it’s the only completely irregular -er verb. Learn it by heart: it’s one of the most used verbs.
Where are you going? Use the contractions from chapter 3, plus “chez” for a person:
I’m going to the office. (à + le)
Are you going to the bakery?
We’re going to the United States. (à + les)
She’s going to the doctor’s. (to a person: chez)
Shall we go to my place?
“Ça va ?” from chapter 1 is actually the verb aller: “does it go?”. And “Allez !” = “Come on!”, while “On y va !” = “Let’s go!”.
The time is always given with “Il est” + number + “heure(s)”. Unlike English “o’clock”, the word “heures” is never left out.
Like “to” in English, “moins” (minus) counts back from the next hour: “neuf heures moins dix” = “ten to nine”. And “et quart / et demie” = “quarter past / half past”.
“Il est une heure” (one o’clock) is singular. And careful: “Quelle heure est-il ?” = “What time is it?”, but “À quelle heure ?” = “At what time?”: “À quelle heure est la réunion ? — À dix heures.”
The days are masculine and written with a small letter: lundi = Monday, mardi = Tuesday, mercredi = Wednesday, jeudi = Thursday, vendredi = Friday, samedi = Saturday, dimanche = Sunday.
Le lundi, il y a une réunion.
Don’t put a preposition before the day (no “on Monday”): “Je travaille lundi”, not “en lundi”. The day stands alone or with “le”.
Time words: aujourd’hui (today), demain (tomorrow), hier (yesterday), le matin (in the morning), l’après-midi (in the afternoon), le soir (in the evening), le week-end, la semaine (the week).

Up to 69 everything is logical: vingt (20), trente (30), quarante (40), cinquante (50), soixante (60). For 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 you say “et un”: vingt et un. Otherwise use a hyphen: vingt-deux, trente-cinq.
From 70 on, French counts in twenties, as in the days of the Gauls:
In Belgium and Switzerland it’s simpler: septante (70), nonante (90), and in Switzerland also huitante (80). The French understand you, but they use the forms above.
“Quatre-vingts” (80) has an -s, but “quatre-vingt-un” (81) doesn’t: the s appears only when no other number follows.

For schedules you use “commencer” (to start, a regular -er verb) and “finir” (to finish). “Finir” belongs to the second group; for now remember the forms: je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent.
The shop is open from nine to seven.
“De … à …” = “from … to …”: “Je travaille du lundi au vendredi” (I work from Monday to Friday). Watch the contractions: du = de + le, au = à + le.
